6f837885.body:
If you're on Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro and your stomach feels like it's full of cement, you can't stop burping sulfur, and you haven't had a normal bowel movement in weeks, I need you to hear this.

Because what I'm about to tell you is going to make you furious.

Here's what's happening right now:

One — The medication that's finally silencing your food noise is quietly wrecking your digestion from the top down. Not just "causing constipation." Something deeper.

Two — When you bring it up to your doctor, they're going to tell you to take Miralax and drink more water.

And three — There's a reason that advice doesn't work. And a reason nobody's telling you why.

I know this because I've watched it happen from the other side of the exam room.

I've been a nurse for 23 years. I've seen things that would make you lose sleep. But the thing I can't stop thinking about is a 58-year-old woman named Karen who sat on the exam table in our clinic and cried because she hadn't had a bowel movement in eleven days.

Let me tell you what happened to her.

She'd been on Wegovy for five months. Down 31 pounds. Bloodwork was beautiful. A1C improved. Blood pressure down. On paper, she was a textbook success.

I took her vitals and asked the standard questions. She answered everything fine until I asked, "Any digestive issues?"

And she just... stopped talking. Looked at the floor. Then looked at me with this expression I've seen a thousand times — the one where someone is deciding whether to tell the truth or say what they think the doctor wants to hear.

"I haven't gone to the bathroom in eleven days," she said.

I put down my clipboard.

She started talking fast, the way people do when they've been holding something in. The bloating so severe she couldn't button her pants. The sulfur burps that smelled like rotten eggs — so bad her grandson had commented on her breath at his baseball game in front of the whole bleacher section. The pressure in her stomach that kept her up at night. The feeling of food from dinner still sitting there the next morning, like a brick that wouldn't dissolve.

She told me about the enemas. Plural. That she'd given herself one at a gas station bathroom during a road trip because the pain was a ten out of ten and she couldn't make it to her daughter's house.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. Miralax. Dulcolax. Colace. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Senna. Smooth Move tea. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice.

She told me she had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

Then she said the thing I hear from every one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted for thirty years. But she's too sick to enjoy living in it.

Sound familiar?

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. I know because I checked.

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber and trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Follow up in six weeks.

She left. I walked her out. At the door she turned and said, "He didn't hear a single thing I said, did he?"

I wanted to tell her the truth. Instead I said, "Give the Linzess a try and call us if it doesn't help."

She didn't call back. They never do. Because the weight is still coming off. And they've decided the suffering is the price of admission.

But Karen broke something in me. Because she wasn't the first. She was just the one who made me stop handing out the same useless advice and start asking why it never worked.

So I started researching. Not patient forums. Not Facebook groups. The actual studies.

And what I found at 1 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table, made me want to walk back into that exam room and apologize to every woman I'd ever handed a Miralax recommendation to.

Because we were all treating the wrong organ.

Think of digestion as a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp — the stomach. Travels through the middle — the small intestine. Exits at the off-ramp — the colon.

When you hear "constipation," you think colon. Everyone does. That's where things exit. That's where the blockage must be.

But GLP-1 medications don't work at the off-ramp. They slow things down at the on-ramp. The stomach loses its rhythm. Food sits there for hours — sometimes days. It ferments. That's where the sulfur gas comes from. It dries out and hardens. That's the cement feeling.

By the time anything reaches the colon — if it reaches the colon — it's already a brick. The colon isn't blocked. It's empty. The problem was never at the exit.

And every product in Karen's medicine cabinet was aimed at the exit.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften what's sitting there. But nothing was sitting there. The blockage was in her stomach, six feet upstream.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

Dulcolax forces the colon to contract. But you can squeeze an empty tube all day long. Nothing comes out if nothing went in.

Smooth Move tea stimulates the lower intestine. Same problem. You can't flush a pipe from the bottom when the clog is at the top.

So the question became: what actually works on the stomach?

I spent three nights on PubMed. Followed citations from paper to paper. Three things kept surfacing.

First — a compound found in high concentrations in celery. Apigenin.

It supports the vagus nerve — the nerve that controls stomach contractions, the nerve that tells the stomach when to push food through. GLP-1 medications essentially mute that signal. Apigenin was showing up in motility studies as a way to gently support it again. Not override the medication. Not force anything. Like turning the volume back up on a speaker someone turned down.

That was the first piece. Get the stomach moving again.

But even with the stomach moving, there's a backlog. Weeks of slow digestion mean bacteria have been producing hydrogen sulfide — sulfur gas — faster than the body can clear it. Getting things moving doesn't fix the gas that's already forming.

The second piece was chlorophyllin — a concentrated form of chlorophyll that binds directly to hydrogen sulfide and neutralizes it before it rises as gas. Doesn't mask the smell. Disarms the molecule that creates it.

Two pieces. But I kept reading. Because even with the stomach moving and the gas handled, everything downstream is backed up too. Weeks of stalled motility mean the small intestine and colon are congested.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume to the gridlock. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Karen's medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Every product addressed one piece — and most of them addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system.

Everything had one piece. Nothing had all three in the right form.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of. They'd built a gummy — specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyll. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber. I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. At concentrations that matched the research.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I called her the next day. She'd stopped coming to our clinic — I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

That text shouldn't have hit as hard as it did.

But it did. Because I knew about the eleven days. The gas station. The spreadsheet. The baseball game.

Week three — the sulfur burps were nearly gone. I thought about her grandson at the baseball game. The whole bleacher section. That didn't have to happen. None of it did.

"I had coffee with my friend Linda this morning," she said. "I didn't think about my breath once. Do you know how long it's been since that happened?"

Month one — she stopped by the clinic. Not as a patient. To see me. She'd thrown out the spreadsheet. Still on Wegovy. Still losing weight. Still had the silence where food didn't run her brain.

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

Month two — her husband noticed she was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time.

I've since shared the same research with four other patients. Quietly. On my own time. Every one had the same pattern — weeks of nothing from laxatives, then steady improvement once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon.

Here's what I need you to hear — from a nurse who has watched this happen over and over:

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. That's not a mystery. That's mechanics. And until something addresses all three, you can take every laxative in the pharmacy and still end up on day eleven with a spreadsheet and an enema kit in your purse.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. You don't have to accept the tax.

Karen didn't.

And she's back at the baseball games.

 EDIT: Adding this once so I can stop answering the same DM: the link to Motilli is here. And one more thing, for the women scrolling past this thinking "I just deal with it." That is word for word what Karen said on the exam table. Dealing with it isn't a plan. You don't have to pay the tax.

758822b3.body:
I had a constipation crisis somewhere over the Atlantic, on the way to my son's wedding in Germany. 3 days later, a village doctor outside Munich asked me 1 question that made my American gastroenterologist look 15 years behind.

I'm 58 years old.

My son met a German girl in graduate school. They planned the wedding for her family's town in Bavaria, a little place an hour outside Munich. We booked the flights 11 months in advance.

I had one job that week: be the mother of the groom.

Instead, by the time the seatbelt light went off over the Atlantic, my gut had already shut down.

If you have what I have, you know exactly what flying does. The dehydration, the sitting, the schedule flipped upside down. Travel seals me shut.

I hadn't gone in 2 days when we boarded.

By the rehearsal dinner, it was 6.

I sat at a long wooden table in a beautiful restaurant while a room full of people I'd just met toasted my son, and the whole time there was a hard knot under my ribs and a waistband cutting into a belly that felt like a drum.

I smiled through all of it.

I've had a lot of practice.

Here's something I had never said out loud before that week: I hadn't talked honestly about being backed up in 5 years. Not with a friend. Not with my husband, not in any detail. Not even with my gastroenterologist beyond the same 3 sentences at every checkup.

She has me on MiraLAX. Every morning. 2 years now. Before that it was fiber, which made everything worse.

The morning after the rehearsal dinner I woke up doubled over. Sharp cramps. Sweating through my blouse before breakfast.

My husband took one look at me and said, "That's it. We're finding you a doctor. Today."

I didn't argue. The wedding was in 2 days and I could not stand up straight.

The bride's mother made one phone call. That's how small the town is. There's a doctor's practice on the main street, above the bakery.

Dr. Brandt. Late fifties. Rimless glasses. English better than my college roommate's.

She pressed along my abdomen. Asked me to lie back. Asked questions nobody had asked me in years.

"The immediate problem is 6 days of travel, airplane dehydration, rich food," she said. "That I can help with today. But this is not new. How long have you been chronically backed up?"

"About 5 years," I said. "My gastroenterologist has me on MiraLAX every morning."

She nodded slowly.

Then she asked the question.

"Has anyone ever looked at the signal? Not the stool. The signal that tells your colon to move."

I stared at her.

"The what?"

She set down her pen.

"Your colon is a muscle wrapped in nerves," she said. "Millions of them, woven through the wall. The muscle never moves on its own. It contracts when those nerves fire, in a wave, top to bottom. When a woman tells me her constipation crept in around menopause and has slowly worsened for years, and that every laxative works for a while and then stops, the muscle is almost never what failed. I start looking at the signal, and whether it has gone quiet."

"And the scoop you take every morning does nothing for that signal. It pulls water into the colon and pushes the load through with volume. It clears today. The nerves that should run tomorrow are exactly as quiet as they were yesterday. So next year you need more scoop. You have felt this already, yes?"

I had. My dose had crept from 1 capful to 2. I'd never told anyone that either.

"My gastroenterologist has never said one word about a signal," I said.

Dr. Brandt shrugged, not unkindly.

"American GI practice just isn't set up that way. The training there is structure and output. Scopes, scans, laxatives, then prescriptions like Linzess when the laxatives fail. Here we've talked about chronic constipation as a nerve and rhythm problem for a long time. It's a different starting point."

She gave me something for the immediate crisis. It worked. I stood at my son's wedding in the dress I'd bought for it, and if you look at the photos you can't tell anything was wrong, as long as you don't look too closely at how I'm holding my clutch.

But I couldn't stop thinking about the question.

5 years. Checkups every 6 months. A dose that quietly doubled.

And not one person had ever mentioned the thing the German doctor considered so basic she almost seemed surprised I hadn't heard it.

We flew home on a Monday.

The night we unpacked, I opened my laptop.

It was 11:45 PM.

I started searching.

"nerve signal colon contraction"

"why constipation starts at menopause"

"slow transit constipation signal"

At 1:30 AM, I was reading about the wave that moves the healthy colon, strongest in the first hour after waking. About the net of nerves in the gut wall that doctors call the second brain. About what every nerve impulse in the human body actually runs on: mineral salts. Sodium and potassium crossing the nerve wall. That is physically what a signal is.

And about estrogen. How it supports the whole system, and what happens to gut motility when it drops.

I sat back in my chair.

My constipation started the year my periods ended. I had told my gastroenterologist that, 5 years ago, and she had written "chronic constipation" in my chart and reached for the scoop.

Nobody connected it. The German doctor connected it in 4 minutes.

Somewhere after 2 AM I found my way to the celery juice women.

I want to be honest here, because this is the part where I almost closed the laptop.

I had actually tried celery juice before. 4 years ago, when it was everywhere. 16 ounces, fresh, first thing in the morning, empty stomach. And here's the part I'd forgotten until I was reading those threads at 2 AM: it helped. My mornings got easier. I was less bloated.

I lasted 11 days.

Because a bunch of celery a day, a juicer to scrub every morning, celery going slimy in the fridge by Thursday, 20 minutes of prep before work. By day 11 it felt like a second job. I quit, the mornings went back to what they were, and I filed the whole thing under trends I fell for.

Reading at 2 AM, it finally made sense why it had worked.

Celery is one of the most mineral-salt-dense foods there is. The exact salts a nerve fires on. It also carries a compound called mannitol that draws water into the gut gently, alongside the salts, instead of flooding it the way a scoop of laxative powder does. Taken on an empty stomach, first thing, it lands during the 1 hour a day the colon is built to fire.

I'd stumbled onto the right answer 4 years ago and quit it because the delivery method was impossible.

At 2:50 AM I started looking at powders.

Most of them were exactly what I feared. "Celery powder" that's the whole stalk, dried and ground into dust. Mostly fiber, which is the last thing a stalled gut needs. Or scoops so small, 2.5 grams, that reviewers said it tasted like water. Or blends where celery sat ninth on an ingredient list behind 3 kinds of grass.

And then, on the second page of results, a 1-ingredient label stopped me. Motilli.

Celery juice solids. The fiber already removed, the salts kept. A 5,000 milligram scoop. The ingredient list is 1 line: celery juice powder. Nothing else in the pouch.

I read every review on the page. Women my age. Same story as mine, some of them almost word for word. The scoop that stopped working. The doctor who shrugged. Mornings that came back in 2 or 3 weeks.

I ordered it at 3:15 AM.

When it arrived, I started the next morning.

1 scoop in a glass of water, before coffee, before food. 60 seconds. No juicer. Nothing to scrub.

Week 1, the constant low cramping I'd carried for years was quieter. I didn't trust it yet.

Week 2, I sat down 1 morning and went. On my own. No scoop. For the first time in 5 years. It happened again 2 days later. And again.

Week 4, I was going most mornings. The bloat was gone by 9 AM instead of bedtime. My pants fit on Friday the same way they fit on Monday. The hard knot under my ribs was gone.

Somewhere in there I stopped adding the MiraLAX to my coffee. Not as a decision. I just kept forgetting it, the way you forget an umbrella once it stops raining.

At 3 months, I had my regular checkup with my gastroenterologist.

She looked at my chart. Then at me.

"Your bowel habits are significantly improved. That's unusual after 5 years of slow transit. What changed?"

"I stopped the MiraLAX 2 months ago."

Her head came up. "You stopped?"

"A doctor in Germany told me my colon wasn't a plumbing problem. It was a signal problem. I found something that feeds the signal instead of forcing the muscle."

She was quiet for a moment.

"Well. The results speak for themselves. Keep doing whatever you're doing."

I left her office feeling something I hadn't felt in years.

Aware, I think, is the word.

My gastroenterologist wasn't hiding anything from me. She was doing exactly what she was trained to do. Manage the output. Escalate when it fails.

The signal was never part of her training.

It took a doctor above a bakery in Bavaria, 4 minutes, and 1 question.

I'm 58. My mornings are mine again. And this September we're flying back to Germany to visit the kids, and for the first time in 5 years I am not packing a pharmacy in my carry-on.

If your doctor has you on a daily scoop, and the dose has crept, and nobody has ever once mentioned the signal that actually moves your colon, you now know what I know.

The brand I use is Motilli. Celery juice solids, 5,000 milligrams per scoop, single ingredient. 1 scoop in water, first thing in the morning, empty stomach. They give you 90 days to try it, and if your mornings don't change, you send it back and get your money back.

I don't get anything from sharing this.

I just know what it's like to smile through your own son's rehearsal dinner while your body holds you hostage.

And I know what it's like to have a stranger in another country explain your own gut to you in 4 minutes, when your specialist of 5 years never mentioned the one thing that turned out to matter.

https://getmotilli.com

P.S. There's a photo from the wedding week my husband took before I saw the doctor. I'm standing apart from the group with my clutch pressed flat against my stomach like a shield. Last month, at our anniversary dinner, I ate a 3-course meal and he looked at me across the table and said, "You're not bracing anymore." I'd been bracing for so long I didn't know I was doing it.

1e3c8e6c.body:
After 7 years on daily MiraLAX, I sat in a motility specialist's office at 55 years old, terrified she was about to confirm what every doctor before her had hinted at.

That I'd permanently destroyed my own colon.

She didn't say that.

What she told me next is the reason I'm writing this.

Because if you've been on MiraLAX or magnesium or anything stronger for more than a year, and somewhere in the back of your head there's a quiet voice telling you that you've done something to your body that can't be undone, I need you to read this whole thing.

I almost didn't write it.

My name is Linda.

I'm 55 years old.

I work in HR for an insurance company in Hartford, Connecticut.

I've been married to my husband Mark for 29 years.

From the outside, my life looks like the life I always wanted.

But for the last 7 years, the most important fact of my life has been the white bottle of MiraLAX on the second shelf of my bathroom cabinet.

I want to tell you about the last year of those 7, because it's the year I became convinced I had permanently destroyed my own colon.

If any of what I describe sounds familiar to you, please don't stop reading until you get to the part about the doctor.

Because she told me something I needed to hear 7 years ago.

She told me something I think you need to hear right now.

I'm going to start with how I got here, but I'm going to keep it short, because the way you got here is probably similar.

I turned 48 in the summer of 2018.

My periods stopped that fall.

A few months after that, I noticed I wasn't going to the bathroom every day anymore.

Then every other day.

Then twice a week.

I went to my GP, a man who'd been my doctor since I was 30.

He said, and I'm quoting him: "Try a capful of MiraLAX in your morning coffee. It's totally safe. Doesn't cause any issues. You can take it as long as you need to."

I trusted him.

I went home and started taking it.

I was 48 years old.

For about a year, it worked.

A capful in the morning, by 10 o'clock my body would do what it was supposed to do, and I'd forget about it for the rest of the day.

Then it stopped being enough.

I went to 2 capfuls.

Then I added magnesium powder at night, mixed in water.

Then on the bad weeks I started taking Dulcolax.

Then there weren't really good weeks anymore, just less-bad ones.

By the summer I turned 54, I was on MiraLAX in the morning, magnesium at night, and Dulcolax 3 or 4 times a week.

That summer was when the fear started.

Up until then I'd been telling myself a story.

The story was: this is a problem I'm managing, like blood pressure, like cholesterol.

I take my doses, my body works, life continues.

That story stopped being available to me in July of last year, and I want to tell you exactly when it broke.

I was sitting up in bed at 2 AM.

Mark was asleep next to me.

I had taken my normal evening doses 6 hours earlier.

Nothing had happened.

I had been bloated all day.

I'd taken an extra Dulcolax at 11 PM out of panic.

Still nothing.

I was sitting there in the dark on my phone, and I had just Googled the words "cathartic colon."

If you don't know what cathartic colon is, don't Google it tonight.

Read the rest of this first.

Because what I read at 2 AM that night was the beginning of the worst 12 months of my life.

Cathartic colon, in the way it gets described online, in old medical literature, on the threads I'd read, is what happens when your colon has been chemically pushed for so long that it stops answering.

The muscles stop contracting.

The colon goes dead.

And the only treatment, the women writing online said, was surgery.

A partial colectomy.

They take the dead section out and reconnect what's left.

Some women in those threads had had this done at 60.

Some at 55.

Some at 48.

I sat in bed and read every single thread I could find, and then the page after that, and then the page after that.

I read women describing recoveries.

I read women describing complications.

I read one woman, and I will not forget this for the rest of my life, describing what it's like to live with a permanent colostomy bag at 52.

I closed my phone at 4:30 AM.

I did not sleep.

That night didn't really leave me for the next 12 months.

Every dose I took, I thought about it.

Every time the dose didn't work, I thought about it harder.

I started checking my abdomen in the mirror obsessively, looking for distortion, looking for hardness, looking for the shape of something that had stopped working.

Once, that fall, I tried to stop.

Cold turkey.

I made it 3 days before I had gained 6 pounds of water weight and could not button a single pair of pants I owned.

I went back on the MiraLAX.

I never tried again.

I made an appointment with my GP, the one who'd put me on MiraLAX 7 years before.

I told him I was scared I'd damaged myself.

He looked at my chart.

He said: "Your bloodwork looks fine. You had a colonoscopy at 50, that was clean. You're okay. Just keep doing what you're doing. We don't really have great options for chronic constipation."

I drove home from that appointment crying.

He'd been kind about it, and somehow the kindness made it worse.

He'd told me there was nothing else.

He'd basically told me this was just my life now.

The MiraLAX.

The bottle in the cabinet.

All of it.

Forever.

I want to skip ahead now, to the day everything changed.

It was a Wednesday in May.

I had taken my full evening stack the night before, magnesium powder and 2 Dulcolax, and woken up Tuesday morning to nothing.

I'd added another capful of MiraLAX Tuesday morning.

Nothing.

By Tuesday evening I was so bloated I couldn't button my work pants.

I took an extra Dulcolax Tuesday night.

Nothing.

Wednesday morning I woke up at 5:30 and lay in bed with my hand on my stomach, and I could feel it.

It was hard.

It was distended.

It had not moved in 4 days despite everything I had thrown at it.

And the thought that came into my head, lying there in the dark, was: this is it.

This is the day my body finally stopped responding.

I have killed it.

I told Mark I needed to go to urgent care.

He offered to come with me.

I told him no. I didn't want him to see what was about to happen.

I drove myself to the urgent care on Farmington Avenue.

I sat in the waiting room for an hour and a half.

When the doctor saw me, a woman maybe in her forties, in scrubs, tired, I told her I thought I had an obstruction.

I told her about the 7 years.

I told her about the doses.

I told her I had not had a bowel movement in 4 days despite every laxative I owned.

She sent me for an abdominal X-ray.

I waited another 40 minutes.

She came back into the exam room with the result on a tablet.

She turned the screen toward me.

She said, "There's no obstruction. You have a significant amount of stool throughout your colon, but no obstruction. Your colon is just being sluggish today. I'd recommend a stronger dose tonight. Maybe try an enema if it's not moving by tomorrow."

I sat on the exam table and stared at her.

I had been preparing, for an hour and a half in the waiting room, for her to tell me my colon was dead.

I had been preparing for surgery.

I had been preparing for the worst.

What she'd told me was almost worse.

She had told me nothing was wrong.

That what I was experiencing, the bloat, the not-going, the 4 days of nothing, was just a normal Tuesday for me now.

That I should take more.

I drove from the urgent care to an empty parking lot and sat in my car for 45 minutes and cried.

This is what I want every woman reading this to understand.

I sat in that parking lot crying because no one in medicine was going to help me.

I had been to my GP, who told me I was fine.

I had been to an urgent care, who told me to take more.

I had had a colonoscopy at 50 that came back clean.

I had had bloodwork that came back clean.

The system had nothing else to offer me.

And I was certain, in a way I'd been certain for almost a year, that I had broken something inside me that was not going to come back, and I was going to have to live with it.

I went home.

I told Mark what had happened.

He sat down on the couch next to me and held my hand and said:

"There has to be a doctor somewhere who treats this. There has to be a specialist. Let's find one."

So we started searching.

What I learned in the days that followed is that most gastroenterologists treat structural problems. Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, polyps, cancer screening, hemorrhoids.

There's a smaller subspecialty within gastroenterology called motility.

Motility doctors focus on how the gut moves, rather than what it looks like.

Most major university hospitals have 1 or 2 motility specialists on staff.

Most regional hospitals have none.

The one Mark found was Dr. Ruth Calloway.

She had completed her gastroenterology training at the Cleveland Clinic in the 1990s and stayed there for the first decade of her career doing research on the nerve activity that drives the human colon.

She moved to Connecticut in 2013 to build the motility program at the university hospital here.

Her clinic was 8 weeks out for new patients.

She did not advertise.

She took referrals only from primary care physicians or other gastroenterologists.

Mark got my GP to write the referral letter the day after I came home from urgent care.

The reason we found her at all was that a woman in Mark's office had a sister-in-law who'd been her patient 3 years earlier and would not stop talking about her.

That is how rare this kind of doctor is.

The 8 weeks of waiting were ordinary. I did what I had been doing for 7 years.

I want to take you to the morning of the appointment.

It was a Tuesday in July.

I had myself fully prepared for what Dr. Calloway was going to tell me.

I had Googled "cathartic colon" probably 100 more times in the 8-week wait.

I was convinced she was going to look at my chart, run a test, and tell me my colon was structurally damaged.

That maybe I'd need surgery in 5 years.

That I had done this to myself and now I had to live with it.

I went in expecting the death sentence I had been preparing for since the previous July.

The waiting room had a poster about colon cancer awareness on one wall and a fake plant in the corner.

When she walked into the exam room, the first thing I noticed was that she was about my age.

Late fifties.

Short gray hair.

Wire-rimmed glasses.

She sat down on the rolling stool, opened her laptop, and read my chart in silence for almost 2 full minutes.

Then she looked up at me and asked:

"When was the last time you had a bowel movement without taking anything?"

I sat there trying to count back.

I couldn't.

The honest answer was I genuinely could not remember the last time my body had done that on its own.

She watched me try to count, and then she said, very quietly:

"It's okay. I want you to know that I see this pattern every single week, multiple times a week. Women your age. Women younger than you. You are not unusual. And you are not broken in the way you think you are."

I started crying right there in the exam room.

I had spent a year preparing for the opposite sentence.

She handed me a tissue and she waited.

Then she said: "I want to run 1 test on you today, just to confirm severity. But I want you to understand something before I do. I have already heard enough from you to know what's going on. The test won't change my diagnosis. It'll only tell me how far along it is."

She ordered a sitz marker test.

You swallow a capsule containing 24 small radio-opaque markers, and they take X-rays at 24, 48, and 72 hours to see how many have moved through your system.

"Come back in 3 weeks. We'll go over the result."

3 weeks later I was back.

She came in with a folder and sat down and said, "I want to walk you through what's been happening to you. And I'm going to take some time with this. Because nobody has probably explained it to you this way before."

Here is what she told me.

I'm going to do my best to reproduce it the way she said it, because I have replayed this conversation in my head 100 times since.

She started by drawing a circle on a notepad.

"This is your colon."

She drew a band of small lines all the way around the outside of the circle.

"Wrapped through the wall of your colon, there's a net of nerves. Millions of nerve cells. Doctors sometimes call it the second brain. Its job is to send one message to the muscle, over and over, all day long: contract, relax, contract, relax. That wave is what moves everything through you."

She paused.

"The muscle only contracts when the message arrives. No message, no movement. It's that simple, and almost nobody explains it to patients."

She made a fist and slowly opened it.

"This is what your colon muscle does when the message arrives. Contract, relax. That's called peristalsis."

She held her fist closed.

"In the pattern you're describing to me, the dose-stacking, the progressive failure of every laxative class, the bloating pattern, the muscle is fine. The nerves are still there. The message has gone quiet. Your colon didn't die. The message just stopped arriving."

I had to ask her to slow down.

She did.

She said: "Your sitz marker test showed you retained 21 of 24 markers at 72 hours. That puts you in the severe slow-transit category. Most healthy adults retain fewer than 5 at 72 hours."

I knew the number was bad.

Hearing her say it made me feel sick.

"Here's what's happened over the last 7 years. Every time you've taken a stimulant laxative, your Dulcolax, it whips the muscle into a contraction directly. You get a bowel movement. But it does nothing for the signal. The signal stays quiet."

She paused.

"And every time you've taken MiraLAX, you've drawn water into the colon and pushed material through with sheer volume. You may get through today. But the rhythm that should run tomorrow still never fires."

Another pause.

"And the magnesium? The reason it stopped working is that it's the same idea in a different bottle. Water, pressure, volume. 7 years of forcing today's load. 7 years of never restoring tomorrow's signal."

I asked her the question I had asked 4 doctors over 7 years:

"Why couldn't anyone else see this?"

She gave me a tired smile.

"Because we don't think about it this way in mainstream gastroenterology. The standard workup looks at structure. Your colonoscopy looked at the walls of your colon, which were normal. It doesn't look at whether the rhythm is firing. And most of us were never trained to think about chronic constipation as a signal problem."

Then she said the thing I want every woman reading this to hear.

I want you to read it twice if you have to.

She said: "What you have is real. It is diagnosable. And it is reversible. You have not destroyed your colon. The signal went quiet, and a quiet signal can be brought back."

I am not going to pretend I didn't sob.

I had spent a year in a private hell of believing I had broken something inside my body that couldn't be repaired.

A year of 2 AM Googling.

A year of looking at my abdomen in the mirror and seeing a body I had ruined.

A year of preparing for surgery.

And in 1 sentence, a doctor I had known for 25 minutes had taken all of it back.

Then she said: "But I have to tell you the rest of it. Because the part you haven't heard yet is the most important."

She said: "There's a reason the signal hasn't come back on its own, even on the weeks you went easier on the laxatives. Nerves don't run on willpower. They run on chemistry. Every nerve impulse in your body, including the one that moves your colon, fires on mineral salts. Sodium and potassium moving across the nerve wall. That is what a nerve signal physically is."

She tapped the notepad.

"When you were younger, your hormones kept that whole system turned up. Estrogen supports the signal. When your periods stopped at 48, the signal dropped. You told me yourself the constipation started a few months later. That timing wasn't a coincidence. That was the volume being turned down."

She looked at me.

"So the question isn't how to force the muscle one more time. You've spent 7 years proving that works less every year. The question is how to feed the signal."

I asked her how.

She said: "3 things have to happen. In this exact order."

She held up one finger.

"First, you have to give the nerves the raw material they fire on. The mineral salts. Every morning. In a form that actually reaches the gut."

Second finger.

"Then you have to do it consistently enough that the rhythm has a chance to re-establish. A signal is a habit. It comes back the way it left. Gradually."

Third finger.

"And you have to do it gently, without turning your morning into another emergency."

She looked at me.

"Stimulants fail the third step. They can force a movement, but they create cramps, urgency, and more fear."

"Osmotic laxatives fail the first step. They move water. They feed nothing."

"Fiber fails on a gut like yours because bulk on top of a stalled system just adds to the pile. You've felt that already."

She paused.

"There are not many everyday foods that deliver the right salts, in the right ratio, in a form most women will actually take every single morning."

Then she told me about celery juice.

I actually laughed. I thought she was joking.

She didn't laugh.

She said: "I know exactly how this sounds. I'm a board-certified gastroenterologist. I spent 20 years prescribing prokinetics. I would have rolled my eyes at this in 2012. Then I started paying attention to what it actually is. Celery is one of the most mineral-salt-dense foods a person can consume. It also carries a compound called mannitol that draws water into the gut gently, alongside the salts, instead of flooding it the way a scoop of polyethylene glycol does. The women who drink it fresh, first thing in the morning, on an empty stomach, are doing something physiologically smarter than they've been given credit for. They're feeding the signal, at the exact hour of the day the colon is built to fire."

She said the morning matters because the colon's strongest natural wave happens in the first hour after waking.

That's why healthy people go in the morning.

That's the window the ritual rides.

Then she held up a hand.

"Here's the honest part. 16 ounces of fresh celery juice a day means a bunch of celery a day, a juicer, and 20 minutes of prep and cleanup every single morning. I have watched hundreds of patients start it and I can count on 2 hands the ones still doing it a year later. The ones who quit didn't quit because it wasn't working. They quit because it's unsustainable. And a signal you feed for 3 weeks and then abandon goes right back to quiet."

I asked her what she actually tells patients to do.

She said: "The version that survives real life is the powder. But you have to read the bag, because most of what's sold as celery powder is the whole stalk, dried and ground. Mostly fiber dust. Almost none of what you need. What you want is the juice solids. The part of the plant the salts and the mannitol actually live in, with the fiber already removed, at a full dose. If the scoop is under a few grams, or the label says anything other than celery juice, put it back."

I wrote that down.

Juice solids. Full dose. Nothing else on the label.

Then I asked the question that had been building in my throat for an hour.

"Do I have to stop the MiraLAX?"

This is the part I want every woman reading this to underline.

Because I know this fear.

I know it because the thought of stopping cold turkey was, in some ways, more terrifying than anything she had said up to this point.

I had tried, the previous fall, and I had made it 3 days.

She said: "Absolutely not. You keep taking your MiraLAX. We do not change anything in your current protocol on day 1."

She said: "Here's what's going to happen. You're going to take the celery juice solids every morning, 1 scoop in a glass of water, first thing, empty stomach. You continue everything else as normal. Over the first 3 to 4 weeks, as the signal starts to come back, your own motility will start to come back. As it does, and you will feel this, you will naturally need less and less MiraLAX. Your body will tell you. We don't taper on a schedule. We taper on response."

I started crying again.

I had not realized, until that moment, how badly I needed somebody to tell me I did not have to choose between the laxatives that had scared me half to death and the terror of withdrawing from them.

That I could keep my safety net.

That my body would be the one to tell me when to put it down.

She walked me out.

It was a sunny Tuesday in July.

I sat in my car in the parking garage for almost 40 minutes before I drove home.

I had walked into that office with a year of fear sitting in my chest.

I walked out with a different sentence in my head than the one I'd been carrying since the previous July.

That night I went looking for the powder she described.

Most of what I found failed her checklist in the first 10 seconds. Whole dried celery. Blends with fourteen other ingredients. Scoops so small the serving was basically a garnish.

The one that passed was Motilli.

Celery juice solids, 5,000 milligrams per scoop, and the ingredient list is 1 line long. Celery juice powder. Nothing else.

I ordered it that night.

I want to tell you what happened next, but I want to be honest with you about the first 3 weeks.

Because this is the part where people give up.

Week 1: nothing dramatic.

I felt about the same.

I drank it every morning. 1 scoop, a glass of water, before coffee, before food.

I kept the MiraLAX.

I waited.

The only thing I noticed in week 1 was that my bathroom trips were maybe, maybe, slightly less effortful.

Normal-flat, the way mine used to be when I was 47.

I stood in front of the mirror and stared at it.

I went downstairs, made coffee, and didn't add the MiraLAX to it.

I just wanted to see what would happen.

At 9:15 AM, on my own, with no chemical assistance, I had a real bowel movement.

I sat there afterwards and cried for 10 minutes.

I texted Mark.

I just said, "I went on my own."

He wrote back, "Honey."

That's the whole text.

Just: honey.

Week 3: I had 3 unassisted bowel movements that week.

The bloating was noticeably down by mid-afternoon.

I cut the MiraLAX to half a capful in the morning, just as a hedge.

Week 4: I started forgetting my magnesium.

By the time I'd remember, it was 10 PM and I'd think, well, let's see what happens if I don't take it.

The next morning, on my own, I went.

Around week 5 something happened that I didn't connect to any of this until later.

I head up HR at the company.

For the last 3 or 4 years I'd been quiet in meetings.

I'd told myself I was just letting the younger people lead.

The truth was I'd stopped being able to follow conversations in real time.

There was always a sort of fog around my thinking.

A delay.

A feeling like I was watching everyone else from behind a window.

I'd been foggy for so long I'd assumed that was just my brain at 55.

That Tuesday, in a quarterly review, somebody made a point I disagreed with.

I am 55 years old.

My husband is watching me instead of the movie. "Something's wrong. I'm getting someone."

He presses the call button. A flight attendant crouches next to our row, then gets on the intercom: "If there is a physician on board, please make yourself known to the crew."

A woman two rows up stands. Introduces herself in accented English. Dr. Ida Nissen. Danish. A gastroenterologist, on her way home from a conference.

"This is uncomfortable, but you are not in danger," she says. "We do not need to divert. But I would like to talk to you for the rest of this flight, if that's alright."

I nod, because I don't trust my voice yet.

"How long have you been dealing with this?"

"About seven months. Since I started my medication."

"And what has your doctor told you to do?"

"Drink more water. Take a fiber supplement. Use Miralax when it gets bad."

She studies me for a second.

"Has anyone explained to you why you're being told to add fiber, when fiber is exactly the thing your body doesn't have the water to handle right now?"

I stare at her. "What do you mean?"

She sits down in the empty seat across the aisle.

"Your medication slows the muscle that moves food through your gut. That is not a malfunction — it is tied to the exact mechanism suppressing your appetite. You are eating far less. So your fiber intake from actual food has already dropped. The advice is 'add more fiber,' and that sounds correct. But the fiber most people are handed — psyllium, the kind in most standard supplements — swells and gels. It requires water to do that. And you are drinking less, because you are eating less, and for a large number of people on this medication, plain water itself is difficult to tolerate."

"So the fiber sits there. Next to food that is already sitting there, because the muscle that should be moving it has slowed down. Instead of helping, it adds bulk to a system that already has nowhere to put it."

"My gastroenterologist never explained it that way," I said.

She nodded, unsurprised. "In the U.S., the standard advice is fiber and osmotic laxatives, escalating the dose as needed. In Denmark and the Netherlands, GI practices treating this population have moved toward addressing it as three separate mechanical failures happening at once — the motility, the fiber viscosity, and the hydration — rather than one symptom to manage with one product."

"Three failures?"

"The muscle slows, on purpose, as part of how your medication works. Your fiber intake collapses because you're eating so much less. And your hydration collapses right along with your appetite — sometimes made worse because water itself is hard to get down. Treat only one, and the other two keep the problem going. Add a stronger laxative, and you're forcing an already backed-up system, without addressing why it backed up in the first place."

"So what do I do?"

"You need something that nudges the muscle rather than forcing it. A fiber that does not gel or bulk, so it isn't asking you for water you don't have. And something whose entire purpose is making the water you can manage actually go down. Three things, together. Not stronger versions of what you're already doing."

She didn't name a product. She wrote the three things on the back of her boarding pass and handed it to me.

"This isn't obscure information where I practice. It's just not standard conversation in an eight-minute American appointment."

For the rest of the flight, I couldn't stop thinking about it.

Seven months. My doctor had told me to drink more water and eat more fiber, over and over, at every visit. She'd never once mentioned that those two pieces of advice needed to happen together to work, or that the fiber she meant was the wrong kind for someone in my exact situation.

11:52 PM local time.

Three things. Exactly what she'd written on the boarding pass in my bag.
